Dwight was doing his level best not to climb out of his own skin against the far wall. David filed that away and did the math. Go back. Check if Danny had moved on. It was the sensible option — retrace through the pipe hallway, find the first room, see if the stairwell was clear. Simple. Logical. Except that the hallway had somehow doubled in length on their first pass through it, the flashlight had about as much range as a lit match, and the water was still rising with absolutely no indication that it intended to stop. Going back meant navigating all of that in the dark, on a maybe, with no guarantee that anything had changed. It was clearly a bad idea. So was staying where they were and fighting with the immovable wall of furniture. Though... “I mean...” he said, voice low and edged. “...there IS a plan B.” The sound of his boots dragging through the water was louder than the voice in his head telling him this was a bad idea. David scrubbed a hand through his hair, flicking water off his fingers in frustration. Dwight hunched in on himself, flinching again as something bumped his calf for the umpteenth time. He didn’t even bother to hiss a warning this time, just shot a glare into the shadows, flashlight beam jittering with the tremor in his hand. “There’s always the ceiling hole in the pipe hall.” Dwight stared at him like he'd been punched. “The pipe hall?” His voice cracked. “We barely made it through the first time, and now it’s half- flooded and pitch black. Getting past it is one thing, but you want to search it?! What if we miss the hole? What if it’s gone?” “It’s not,” David said, too quickly. Too certain. “But...” “Look, I don’t like it either. But we don’t really have time here. Plus, it’s dark enough that we wouldn’t be seen climbing out into the main hallway.” “David, it’s almost 8 feet up! You might be able to climb that...” Dwight froze as a look of tense guilt washed over David. In a heartbeat, he realized what David was hinting at. “You want to wait out the flood. Let the water get us up there.” Dwight watched his jaw tense as he turned his eyes away. It was a bad decision, clearly. But so was everything else. If Ghostface was still at the other stairs, they wouldn’t see him in time. If they kept trying at these stairs, they would loose precious time needed to search the pipe hallway. Assuming they DID find the hole, they would need to wait out the rising water in the dark. No option felt good, but at least the ceiling hole had less chance of getting them stabbed. Dwight looked at the water sitting dark and patient at his waist, and felt something cold move through him regardless. “God, I hate that that might actually work.” David didn’t press when Dwight hesitated at the corridor, flashlight already trembling in his hand. He knew what was waiting there. They both did. But at the rate the water was rising, they were running out of time to debate routes. The pipe hallway had grown. There was no other explanation for it — the junctions multiplying, familiar valves appearing in unfamiliar arrangements, the walls presenting corners that hadn't existed on the first pass. The flashlight beam caught pipes and more pipes and the occasional burst of weirdly neutral- temperature spray as something gave way overhead, hosing them down without warning before the pressure died and the dark closed back in. The flashlight’s beam cut through the dark like a scalpel, but even in the narrow corridors it was weak. Sickly yellow and wavering, barely enough to outline the pipe-laced walls. Water was already brushing along their ribs now. For Dwight, it felt like it was pulling at him, rising along his stomach with a patient claiming. The water lower down tugged at his ankles lightly, a surreal current leading nowhere that felt determined to pull him away from the walls and back into the darkness. He wasn’t cold. Not really. But he still shook so badly he could hardly keep the light straight. It flickered against the walls as if it was afraid too. Every few steps, something slapped or hissed beside them, busted pipes still spewing from unseen seams. It felt personal. Like the building itself was spitting on them for trespassing. David squinted against it, pushing forward with grim determination. The floor was harder to grip as the water level rose, his own buoyancy making his feet slide slightly with every step. Every pipe they brushed against sent shivers up his spine. To his side, Dwight stumbled and nearly fell. David grabbed his arm without looking. The man may have been taller than him, but he was significantly less stable on his feet. Something brushed against Dwight’s leg again — lower, almost playful in its angle — causing a high sound that he hadn’t meant to make. He jolted. The flashlight spun. Water slapped. “David—” “Yeah, I feel it too.” David muttered. “Just keep moving.” They turned another corner. Somehow it was the same corner as the last one. It had to be. “I think we’re going in circles...” “No. We’re not. The pipes — look — they’re different here.” They weren’t. Neither man would admit it. They just adjusted their direction and pushed on. From somewhere above, the pipes hissed—and with a heavy thump, a jet of water slammed down like a burst fire hose into Dwight’s back, driving him into the wall.
